summary:
Future astronauts on Mars need routes that are safe, timed and have places to stop. We built an interactive 3D Mars globe that plans such EVA routes in Jezero Crater, Perseverance’s landing site.

We chose not to let AI pick the route: in our tests, a small model invented paths even when no safe path existed. Instead, our route engine computes every path on HiRISE 1 m terrain (CTX 20 m where HiRISE is unavailable) with hard rules: no slope above 20°, a safety buffer around hazards and no entry into unmapped terrain. Each route is validated before it is drawn, so unsafe routes are never shown.

Users pick two points or set their own base camp. For each route we report length, maximum and mean slope, ascent and descent; rover-plus-walking travel time checked against the EVA window and the 10 km walk-back limit; and the EVA radiation dose. We also mapped flat, low-hazard rest stations, number those near the route, show the longest gap between them and whether each is sunlit or shaded at the chosen hour.

Our Mission Data panel adds real measurements from Perseverance MEDA (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, UV), Mastcam-Z dust, Curiosity RAD radiation, Mars24 sun position and the nearest Perseverance Raw Images, each with unit and source. Single-point values are labelled “site-wide.” A language model (Gemma) explains the route in plain English using only the engine’s numbers.
details:
NavMavors is an interactive 3D Mars globe that plans safer routes for astronauts and rovers in Jezero Crater, Perseverance’s landing site. It answers the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge by layering data from several NASA missions onto a single route. On the globe or the map, a user picks a start and a destination. They can also set their own base camp, which stays saved, and plan from it to any point. Our route engine then computes the path on a terrain grid of 60 m cells. The grid is built from the Mars 2020 HiRISE elevation mosaic at 1 m per pixel, with CTX elevation data at 20 m where HiRISE is unavailable. A weighted Dijkstra search combines distance with terrain risk such as slope and crater depressions, under hard rules: the target is no slope above 20°, consistent with the design limits of the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle; hazardous cells keep a safety buffer; unmapped terrain is never entered; and every route is checked before it is drawn. If no route meets the 20° limit, NavMavors does not hide the problem. It shows the least-risk route it can find, with a clear warning.

We chose to let code, not AI, make this decision after testing both. On 12×12 grids, a 1.7B language model gave safe answers only 44% of the time and invented a route in every case where no route existed, while our Dijkstra-based engine was correct 100 times out of 100. AI still has a role, but only as an explainer. Gemma 4 runs locally and turns the engine’s measured numbers into a short English explanation of why the route was chosen. It cannot choose or change the route, and a number check compares every number in its text with the route data, with a 2% margin, removing any sentence it cannot support.

Each route comes with the numbers a crew would ask for. We report length, maximum and mean slope, ascent and descent. We estimate travel time with the rover driving at 9 km/h and the crew walking the last 500 m at 3.5 km/h, values based on Apollo LRV speeds and NASA EVA walking studies, and we warn if arrival falls outside the 11:00–15:00 EVA window. We flag any route that goes more than 10 km from base, the walk-back limit from NASA JSC testing for the case where the rover fails. We estimate the EVA radiation dose from Curiosity RAD’s 0.64 mSv/day and compare it with NASA’s 600 mSv career limit. We also split the map into ~1 km tiles and mark flat, low-hazard ones as rest stations. Those within 2 km of the route are numbered in order and shown as sunlit or shaded at the chosen hour, along with the longest stretch without a stop. A Mission Data panel brings together Perseverance MEDA temperature, pressure, wind, humidity and UV, Mastcam-Z dust, Mars24 sun position, Curiosity RAD radiation and the nearest Perseverance Raw Images. It can be filtered by local time and Mars season, and every value shows its unit and source.

The benefit is a planner that is safe by design, explains itself and is honest about its data. Weather and radiation were measured at a single point, so we label them “site-wide” and never let them change the route. A missing value shows “no data”, never a guess. Our intended impact follows from that. A route on Mars is more than a line between two points, and NavMavors turns complex terrain and mission data into routes a mission team can evaluate, with lower-risk paths, open warnings and a reason for every choice. The same approach could support EVA planning, training and education, and it shows a responsible way to use AI in safety-critical work: computation decides, AI explains, and every number is checked. NavMavors does not replace the mission team’s judgment; it gives them clearer information to make it.

We built NavMavors with JavaScript on a Node.js and Express server, a three.js globe with HTML and CSS, and JPL Mars Trek map layers. The route engine is our own weighted Dijkstra implementation, running on a terrain grid we generated from HiRISE and CTX data. We used Python to process MEDA, Mastcam-Z and Raw Images data, and our own implementation of the Mars24 sun-position algorithm, which agrees with MEDA’s measured solar geometry to a median of 2.0°. Gemma 4 runs locally for explanations. Claude (Anthropic) helped us write code and research data sources. Earlier experiments with a 1.7B LiquidAI model on Apple silicon with MLX led to our code-first decision. We worked on team laptops and collaborated through Git and GitHub. Our data comes from USGS Astrogeology, the NASA PDS Atmospheres Node, NASA/JPL-Caltech, NASA GISS, Curiosity RAD (Hassler et al., 2014) and the Mastcam-Z optical depth record (Lemmon, 2026, CC BY 4.0).

Our creativity lies in turning a failed experiment into our core design, and in planning for the astronaut rather than only the rover. Walk-back limits, EVA timing, radiation and sunlit rest stops treat a route as a mission plan, not a line on a map. Throughout, we weighed safety first, then data quality. We use CTX where HiRISE does not reach, keep only the most reliable MEDA wind data from sols 60–290 because the sensor was damaged later, and checked cleaned values against their sources. We also weighed responsible AI and the competition rules: every source is cited, all non-NASA data is openly licensed, AI use is disclosed, and no images of team members under 18 are used.
